title: How to introduce new technology to restaurant staff
seoTitle: Introduce new technology to restaurant staff | ROAL
description: Use scripts, steps, and a rollout plan to introduce new technology to restaurant staff without slowing service or creating pushback.
question: How do I introduce new technology restaurant staff can trust without slowing service down?
answer: Introduce it with a clear reason, a simple demo, and a short trial period. Show staff exactly what changes, what stays the same, and which calls still go to people. For a restaurant phone host, that means testing it on the browser first, then forwarding calls only when you are ready.
summary: A practical way to roll out a new phone host without confusing staff or slowing down service.
intro:
Introducing new technology restaurant staff can trust starts with one thing: show them how it helps the shift, not how smart it sounds. In a restaurant, that usually means fewer ringing phones, cleaner order tickets, and fewer interruptions at the counter.

If you want staff on board, keep it simple. Explain what the new phone host does, what it does not do, and how calls still reach a person when they need to.

sections.h2: How do I explain the new phone host to staff in plain English?
sections.body:
Start with the problem everyone already knows: the phone rings while someone is taking an order, boxing food, or helping a guest at the counter. Then explain the one job the new phone host is taking over.

A simple script for the team:

"The phone host will answer routine calls, take pickup and delivery orders, and send them to the kitchen. If a caller has a complaint, allergy concern, or needs a manager, it sends that to us with a summary."

That phrasing helps because it tells staff three things:
- It handles the repetitive calls.
- It does not replace the team on sensitive calls.
- It sends work to the kitchen in a usable form.

If you use ROAL, you can point out that it reads the live menu, answers hours and address questions, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That is the practical benefit staff can see. Keep the first explanation short. You can go deeper after the rush, when everyone has a minute.

sections.h2: What should I show the team before we go live?
sections.body:
Do a quick walk-through before you forward any calls. Staff usually trust a new tool faster when they can see it work on real restaurant details instead of hearing a sales pitch.

Use this checklist:
1. Play a test call in the browser.
2. Show the menu items it can read.
3. Show how it handles sizes, modifiers, and notes.
4. Show where the ticket appears on the kitchen screen.
5. Show how it passes tricky calls to staff.

A concrete example helps. Say you sell a large pepperoni pizza for $18, a medium for $15, and extra cheese for $2. Show the team a caller saying, "Can I get a large pepperoni with extra cheese, pickup in 25 minutes?" Then let staff see the order come through as a clean ticket.

You can also show what the phone host will not do. It will not take card numbers over the phone. That matters because staff need to know the payment step stays on your normal process. When people know the boundaries, they worry less.

sections.h2: How do I roll it out without confusing the shift?
sections.body:
Treat it like a small change, not a full-house reset. Pick one location or one phone number first if you have more than one store. If you have a single restaurant, start during a slower window, not right in the middle of a rush.

A simple rollout plan:
- Tell the team the day before.
- Pick the exact time forwarding starts.
- Decide who checks the inbox for unanswered questions.
- Tell staff which calls still go to a person.
- Review the first few tickets together.

If your restaurant uses ROAL, setup is designed to be quick. The owner can paste a website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name and city, then test-call the host in the browser before claiming it. That makes it easier to show the team something real.

Here is a useful line for the pre-shift huddle: "For the first week, watch the tickets and tell me if anything sounds off. If the host misses a detail, we fix the menu or FAQ once, and it learns from that."

That last part matters. Staff do not need perfection on day one. They need a process for fixing small issues fast.

sections.h2: What calls should still go to staff, and how do I tell the team?
sections.body:
This is where trust grows. Staff need to know the phone host is not a wall between the restaurant and the caller. It should handle routine work and hand off the rest.

Use a simple handoff rule table:

| Call type | Who handles it |
|---|---|
| Pickup order | Phone host |
| Delivery order | Phone host |
| Hours, address, parking | Phone host |
| Menu question from public pages | Phone host |
| Allergy-sensitive question | Staff |
| Complaint | Staff |
| Catering request | Staff |
| Manager request | Staff |
| Reservation request | Phone host or staff, based on your setup |

When you explain this to the team, use language like: "Anything sensitive goes to us with the caller's name, phone number, and a short summary."

That helps staff feel protected, because they are not being asked to solve every call live while juggling the counter. It also helps them trust that the caller is not being ignored. The handoff is still part of the service.

If the restaurant is short-staffed, this setup can reduce interruptions during the busiest parts of the shift. It is especially useful for the kind of calls that keep repeating: hours, address, parking, menu questions, and order status.

sections.h2: How do I set the phone forward without messing up our main number?
sections.body:
Owners often worry that adding a new phone host means losing control of the restaurant number. It does not have to work that way.

With ROAL, the restaurant keeps its own number. The owner claims the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and then the owner forwards the existing number to it. Forwarding can be all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. You can turn it off any time.

Before you change anything, confirm the forwarding code with your carrier or phone system and test it with a real call. Codes vary by carrier and plan. On many landlines and some carriers, 72 followed by the forwarding number forwards all calls and 73 turns it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. Some carriers also support busy or unanswered call forwarding with separate codes.

A practical checklist:
- Write down your current number.
- Confirm the forwarding code with your carrier.
- Test forward one call first.
- Call the restaurant from another phone.
- Make sure the ticket lands where you want it.

If the test sounds wrong, stop and fix it before the lunch rush. That is better than learning during service.

sections.h2: How do I answer staff concerns about jobs and speed?
sections.body:
Be direct. Most staff do not mind new tools when they understand they are there to remove friction, not create more work.

A good manager script is:

"This is here to take routine phone work off your plate. It is not here to replace anyone on the floor. If it saves us time on the phone, we can spend more time on guests, food, and tickets."

Then answer the concerns one by one:
- Will it slow us down? It should reduce interruptions from routine calls.
- Will it change how orders are entered? It sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.
- Will it handle every call? No. Tricky calls still go to staff.
- Will it take card numbers? No. Payment stays with your normal process.

If the team wants proof, show them the call history and transcript after the first day. That gives them a chance to see what callers asked and what the host answered. It also makes it easier to update the menu or FAQs if something needs to be corrected.

For a busy takeout shop, this often becomes a simple trade: fewer interruptions at the front, more predictable phone handling, and less pressure on the team during the rush.

sections.h2: What should I review after the first week?
sections.body:
Do a short review after a few shifts. The goal is not to grade the team. The goal is to make the new workflow fit your restaurant.

Review these items:
1. Which calls went through cleanly?
2. Which questions landed in the inbox?
3. Did the kitchen tickets read clearly?
4. Did any menu item need a wording fix?
5. Did staff know when to step in?

A worked example can help. Say your average completed order is $28. If the phone host handles 40 completed phone orders in a month, that would be 40 x $0.90, or $36 in usage fees, plus your normal payment flow at pickup. Plug in your own order count and average order size when you review whether the setup makes sense for your store.

This is also when you can compare the setup to other ways of handling calls. Delivery apps commonly take rough commission ranges that are much higher than a per-order phone host fee. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Many monthly AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee whether or not orders come in. ROAL is billed monthly based on completed phone orders, with calls, questions, and test calls free.

takeaways: Explain the change in restaurant terms, not tech terms.
Show staff a real test call before you forward live calls.
Keep sensitive calls with people and routine calls with the phone host.
Use the first week to fix menu wording, FAQs, and handoff rules.
ROAL can handle routine orders while staff keep control of the hard calls.

faq.q: How do I introduce new technology restaurant staff can trust?
faq.a: Show the team exactly what it does for the shift, in plain English. Demo one real call, explain what stays with staff, and give them a simple way to report anything that sounds off. When people see the workflow before it goes live, they usually accept it faster.

faq.q: What is the best way to train staff on a new phone system?
faq.a: Keep the training short and tied to real calls. Walk through pickup orders, menu questions, and handoffs for complaints or allergy concerns. Then review the first day’s call history so the team can see what the phone host handled and what still needs human attention.

faq.q: How do I tell employees the phone host is not replacing them?
faq.a: Say it plainly: it is there to take routine phone work off the counter team, not replace the crew. Emphasize that sensitive calls, manager issues, and anything unusual still go to staff. That message is easier to trust when they can see the rules and the handoff process.

faq.q: What should I check before forwarding my restaurant number?
faq.a: Confirm the forwarding code with your carrier or phone system, then test it with one call. Make sure calls reach the right line, the ticket prints or appears correctly, and you can turn forwarding off when needed. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always verify before service.
